slides.inSimpleWords: Your mutual fund value = (number of units you own) × (today's NAV). When NAV rises, your units become worth more. When NAV falls, they're worth less.

slides.title: Priya's Worry: What If NAV Falls?
slides.storyContext: Priya sees NAV drop from ₹110 to ₹105 one day. She panics: 'My money is disappearing!' Ms. Desai calms her: 'No, it's a market fluctuation. This happens every day. Over 10 years, these swings smooth out.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Daily NAV changes are normal. Think of it like weather: storms happen, but over time, the climate is stable. Long-term investors ignore daily noise.

slides.title: SIP: Investing ₹500 Every Month (Rupee Cost Averaging)
slides.storyContext: Priya says: 'I have ₹500 every month, not ₹10,000 today.' Perfect! Ms. Desai explains SIP—Systematic Investment Plan. You invest the same amount every month. Automatically.

points.label: What is SIP?
points.text: SIP means investing a fixed amount (like ₹500) every month in a mutual fund, automatically. You set it up once; it happens every month.

points.label: Rupee Cost Averaging
points.text: When NAV is high, ₹500 buys fewer units. When NAV is low, ₹500 buys more units. Over time, your average cost per unit is lower than if you invested all at once.

points.label: Removes emotion
points.text: You don't worry about 'Is this a good time to invest?' You just invest every month. This removes fear and greed from investing.

points.label: Compound growth
points.text: Your early investments have 15+ years to grow. Later investments grow less. Together, they compound into wealth.

slides.inSimpleWords: SIP is like saving money in a jar, except instead of cash, you're buying mutual fund units every month, automatically.

image.alt: SIP: Investing ₹500 Every Month (Rupee Cost Averaging) — Mutual Funds & SIP — Investing Made Simple

slides.title: Example: Rupee Cost Averaging in Action
slides.storyContext: Priya invests ₹500 every month for 6 months. The NAV fluctuates: Month 1 (₹100), Month 2 (₹110), Month 3 (₹90), Month 4 (₹85), Month 5 (₹95), Month 6 (₹105). Let's see how she benefits from rupee cost averaging.

example.problem:
Month-by-month SIP:
Month 1: NAV ₹100, she buys 5 units (₹500 ÷ ₹100)
Month 2: NAV ₹110, she buys 4.54 units (₹500 ÷ ₹110)
Month 3: NAV ₹90, she buys 5.55 units (₹500 ÷ ₹90)
Month 4: NAV ₹85, she buys 5.88 units (₹500 ÷ ₹85)
Month 5: NAV ₹95, she buys 5.26 units (₹500 ÷ ₹95)
Month 6: NAV ₹105, she buys 4.76 units (₹500 ÷ ₹105)

Total units after 6 months? Average cost per unit? Current value at NAV ₹105?
example.solution:
Total units = 5 + 4.54 + 5.55 + 5.88 + 5.26 + 4.76 = 30.99 units.
Total invested = ₹500 × 6 = ₹3,000.
Average cost per unit = ₹3,000 ÷ 30.99 = ₹96.78 (much lower than if she'd invested at ₹100 flat).
Current value = 30.99 × ₹105 = ₹3,254.
Gain = ₹254 (8.5% in 6 months, despite NAV fluctuations). She got more units when NAV was low (₹85-₹90), fewer when high (₹105-₹110). This averaging effect locked in gains.

slides.inSimpleWords: SIP automatically buys more units when prices drop and fewer when prices spike. Over time, this brings down your average cost and maximizes gains.

slides.title: Priya's Breakthrough: 'This Is Like Buying on Sale!'
slides.storyContext: Priya suddenly gets it: 'When the market crashes and NAV falls to ₹85, I'm actually getting a discount! More units for my ₹500! That's like buying a shirt on 50% off!' Ms. Desai smiles: 'Exactly. Most investors panic during crashes. SIP investors smile.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Market crashes scare lump-sum investors. But SIP investors love crashes because they get discounts on units. It's a mindset shift.

slides.title: Priya's Real SIP: ₹500/Month for 10 Years
slides.storyContext: Priya starts an SIP of ₹500 every month in a mutual fund. She commits to it for 10 years (until she's 25). Let's see what happens.

example.problem:
Priya invests ₹500 every month for 10 years (120 months) in a mutual fund that averages 12% annual return.
Month 1: NAV ₹100, buys 5 units.
Month 2: NAV ₹102, buys 4.9 units.
Month 3: NAV ₹104, buys 4.8 units.
[This continues...]

Assume average NAV over 10 years is ₹140. How many total units will she have? What will be the total value? Total amount invested?
example.solution:
Total amount invested = ₹500 × 120 months = ₹60,000.
With 12% average returns and rupee cost averaging, her average cost per unit ≈ ₹120 (lower than average NAV ₹140, due to buying more units when NAV is low).
Total units ≈ ₹60,000 ÷ ₹120 = 500 units.
Final value = 500 × ₹140 = ₹70,000.
Gain = ₹70,000 - ₹60,000 = ₹10,000 (16.7% gain over 10 years, about 1.5% annually above inflation).

Note: Real SIP performance varies. Some funds give 15%+ annually; others give 8-10%. The power is in the consistency and time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Start small, stay consistent, and let time do the heavy lifting. Priya's ₹500/month grows into ₹70,000+ without her picking a single stock.

image.alt: Priya's Real SIP: ₹500/Month for 10 Years — Mutual Funds & SIP — Investing Made Simple

slides.title: Types of Mutual Funds: Choose Your Risk
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Are all mutual funds the same?' No! Ms. Desai shows Priya different types based on risk and return.

points.label: Equity Funds (High Risk, High Return)
points.text: Invest mostly in stocks. More risky, but higher returns over 10+ years. Best for young investors with time.

points.label: Debt Funds (Low Risk, Low Return)
points.text: Invest mostly in bonds and fixed deposits. Lower risk, stable returns. Best for short-term or risk-averse.

points.label: Balanced Funds (Medium Risk, Medium Return)
points.text: Mix of stocks and bonds (e.g., 60% stocks, 40% bonds). Good balance of growth and safety.

points.label: Index Funds (Passive, Low Cost)
points.text: Copy a stock market index (like Nifty 50). No fancy fund manager. Very low fees. Consistently matches market returns.

slides.inSimpleWords: High-risk funds can give you big gains but big losses. Low-risk funds are safer but grow slowly. Pick based on how much risk you can handle and when you need the money.

image.alt: Types of Mutual Funds: Choose Your Risk — Mutual Funds & SIP — Investing Made Simple

slides.title: Priya's Fund Selection Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya reads: 'Aggressive Growth Fund up 18%! Conservative Fund up 5%.' She's tempted by aggressive. Ms. Desai asks: 'When do you need this money?' Priya says: '10 years.' Ms. Desai nods: 'Then aggressive is perfect for you. Time absorbs risk.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Young investors with long timelines should pick aggressive (high-risk, high-return) funds. In 10 years, even a 50% crash has time to recover.

slides.title: Example: Equity vs. Debt Fund Choice for Priya
slides.storyContext: Priya is 15. She can invest for 10 years until she's 25. Arjun is 15 too, but he needs the money in 2 years for college. They have different time horizons, so different funds suit them.

example.problem:
Priya (SIP for 10 years) and Arjun (needs money in 2 years) each have ₹1,000 to invest.
Option A: Equity Fund (12% average returns, but -15% swings in bad years).
Option B: Debt Fund (8% average returns, but only -2% swings in bad years).

Who should pick which? Why?
example.solution:
Priya should pick Equity Fund. Even if the fund drops 15% in year 1, she has 9 more years to recover and benefit from long-term growth (12% average). The 10-year horizon shields her from short-term volatility.
Arjun should pick Debt Fund. If he picks Equity and the fund drops 15% in year 1, by year 2 it might recover to -5%. He can't afford the loss so close to his college deadline. Debt Fund's stability (only -2% swings) keeps his college fund safer.
Key: Time horizon determines risk. More time = can handle more risk.

slides.inSimpleWords: Young and have 10+ years? Pick equity (higher returns, can weather downturns). Need money soon? Pick debt (safer, smaller swings).

slides.title: How Diversification Protects You
slides.storyContext: Ms. Desai explains: 'Why does Priya's ₹500 mutual fund investment beat a ₹500 stock pick? Diversification.'

points.label: Single stock risk
points.text: If Priya buys ₹500 of one company's stock and that company fails, she loses everything.

points.label: Mutual fund safety
points.text: Her ₹500 via mutual fund owns tiny pieces of 50 companies. If one fails, 49 others still grow. Her loss is small.

points.label: Real example
points.text: One tech company's stock falls 50% due to bad news. But Priya's mutual fund also owns banks, FMCG, and pharma. Those rise. Her overall fund value might only fall 5%.

slides.inSimpleWords: Putting all eggs in one basket is risky. Spreading them across many baskets (diversification) means one broken basket doesn't ruin you.

image.alt: How Diversification Protects You — Mutual Funds & SIP — Investing Made Simple

slides.title: Fund Performance and Expense Ratio
slides.storyContext: Priya reads online: 'Fund A returned 15% this year. Fund B returned 12%.' She thinks Fund A is better. Ms. Desai cautions her: 'Check the expense ratio. Fund A might charge 2% fees, Fund B only 0.5%.'
slides.inSimpleWords: High returns look great, but high fees eat into them. A fund returning 15% with 2% fees is really 13% net. A fund returning 12% with 0.5% fees is really 11.5% net. Compare net returns, not gross.

slides.title: Expense Ratio and Exit Load Explained
slides.storyContext: Ms. Desai draws two charts: 'Every fund has an expense ratio (annual fee) and some charge an exit load (penalty for selling early).'

points.label: Expense Ratio
points.text: Annual fee charged by the fund for management, admin, etc. Ranges from 0.5% (index funds) to 2.5% (active funds). Deducted automatically from NAV.

points.label: Exit Load
points.text: Penalty if you sell within a certain period (e.g., 1 year). E.g., 1% exit load means selling ₹10,000 units within 1 year costs ₹100. Encourages long-term holding.

points.label: Impact over 10 years
points.text: A 1% annual expense ratio on ₹60,000 invested at 12% returns reduces final wealth by ~₹8,000-10,000. Choose low-cost funds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fees compound. 2% fees over 10 years cost you more than ₹10,000 of potential growth. Lower fees = more money stays with you.

slides.title: Example: Impact of Expense Ratio Over 10 Years
slides.storyContext: Priya is choosing between Fund X (expense ratio 2%, average 12% returns) and Fund Y (expense ratio 0.5%, average 11.8% returns). Which is better after 10 years?

example.problem:
Priya's ₹500/month SIP for 10 years (total ₹60,000).

Fund X: 12% gross return, 2% expense ratio = 10% net return.
Fund Y: 11.8% gross return, 0.5% expense ratio = 11.3% net return.

Estimate final value for each. Which fund ends up ahead?
example.solution:
Fund X (10% net): ₹60,000 invested → Roughly ₹155,000 final value (10% compounded annually).
Fund Y (11.3% net): ₹60,000 invested → Roughly ₹180,000 final value (11.3% compounded annually).
Difference: ₹25,000+ MORE in Fund Y, despite only 0.5% higher net return! Over decades, small fee differences matter massively. Choose low-cost index funds or funds with <1% expense ratio.

slides.inSimpleWords: A 1.5% fee difference sounds small, but on ₹60,000 over 10 years, it costs you ₹25,000+ of gains. Always check expense ratios.

slides.title: Priya's Decision: Index Fund vs. Active Fund
slides.storyContext: Priya learns: 'Index funds like Nifty 50 just copy the market at 0.5% fees. Active funds try to beat the market at 1.5% fees, but usually fail.' She decides: 'Index fund for me. Simpler, cheaper, reliable.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Most active fund managers don't beat the index over 10+ years. Index funds are boring but win. For beginners, start with index funds.

slides.title: Your Turn: Plan Your SIP
slides.storyContext: Now it's your turn. You're in Class 10. You can save ₹300 per month from now until you're 30 (20 years). Assume an average mutual fund return of 10% annually. Roughly, how much will you have? (Simplified: ignore taxes, assume consistent 10% return.)

example.problem:
Your 20-Year SIP Challenge:
₹300 per month for 20 years (240 months).
Assume 10% average annual return.
Total invested = ?
Estimated final value ≈ ?
(Simplified calculation: 10% compounds, you invest monthly.)
example.solution:
Total invested = ₹300 × 240 = ₹72,000.
With 10% annual returns over 20 years, money roughly doubles every 7-8 years (rule of 72). After 14 years, ₹72,000 becomes ~₹150,000. After 20 years, with continued monthly investments, rough estimate ≈ ₹200,000-250,000 (actual depends on timing of investments and exact returns).
Key insight: Your total contribution is ₹72,000. Your final value is 2.7x-3.5x that. The difference (₹128,000-178,000) is investment growth—free money from the market and compound growth!

slides.inSimpleWords: Start young. Invest small amounts consistently. Let compound growth work for 20 years. Turn ₹72,000 of your money into ₹200,000+.

image.alt: Your Turn: Plan Your SIP — Mutual Funds & SIP — Investing Made Simple

slides.title: Challenge: SIP vs. Lump Sum
slides.storyContext: Rohan has ₹12,000. He can invest it all today (lump sum) or invest ₹1,000 every month for 12 months (SIP). The fund averages 10% annual returns but fluctuates: ₹100, ₹110, ₹100, ₹105, ₹95, ₹90, ₹95, ₹100, ₹105, ₹110, ₹115, ₹120 (one NAV per month). Which strategy gets him more money?

example.problem:
Lump Sum: Rohan invests ₹12,000 at Month 1 NAV = ₹100. He gets 120 units. After 12 months, NAV = ₹120. His value = 120 × ₹120 = ₹14,400. Gain = ₹2,400 (20%).

SIP: Rohan invests ₹1,000 every month at each month's NAV. Total units after 12 months? Average cost? Final value?
example.solution:
SIP month-by-month units: ₹1,000÷100=10, 1,000÷110=9.09, 1,000÷100=10, 1,000÷105=9.52, 1,000÷95=10.53, 1,000÷90=11.11, 1,000÷95=10.53, 1,000÷100=10, 1,000÷105=9.52, 1,000÷110=9.09, 1,000÷115=8.7, 1,000÷120=8.33. Total ≈ 116 units. Average cost = ₹12,000 ÷ 116 = ₹103.45.
Final value = 116 × ₹120 = ₹13,920. Gain = ₹1,920 (16%).

Winner: Lump Sum (₹14,400 vs. ₹13,920). But wait—SIP bought more units when NAV was low (₹90-₹95). If the fund had crashed to ₹80 at month 6, SIP would have protected Rohan better. Lump sum wins when markets rise steadily; SIP protects when markets are volatile.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lump sum wins in a rising market. SIP wins in a volatile/falling market because you buy more units at low prices. For most people, SIP is safer because we can't predict markets.

slides.title: Challenge: Compound Growth Over Decades
slides.storyContext: Priya's SIP ₹500/month grows at 12% annually. But let's say she stays invested for 30 years until age 45. How much will she have? How much of that is her own money vs. growth?

example.problem:
Priya's 30-Year SIP:
₹500/month for 30 years (360 months) at 12% annual return.
Total she invested = ?
Estimated final value (using compound growth) ≈ ?
How much is 'free money' from growth?
example.solution:
Total invested = ₹500 × 360 = ₹1,80,000.
With 12% annual compound returns, rough estimate after 30 years ≈ ₹2,000,000-₹2,500,000 (using compound growth formulas).
Growth (free money) = ₹2,000,000 - ₹1,80,000 = ₹1,820,000+ (over 90% of her final wealth came from market growth, not her contributions!).
This is the magic of long-term, consistent investing. Start young, stay disciplined, let compound growth do the work.

slides.inSimpleWords: 30 years of ₹500/month grows into ₹2+ million. You contributed ₹1.8 lakh; the market gave you ₹18+ lakh. This is why starting young matters.

slides.title: Priya's First SIP Milestone: One Year In
slides.storyContext: Priya's first year of ₹500/month SIP is complete. She's invested ₹6,000. Her mutual fund shows ₹6,540 value (9% gain). She's thrilled: 'I'm a real investor now!' Ms. Desai smiles: 'Yes, and the next 9 years will be even more rewarding.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Seeing your first investment gain is motivating. But the real magic happens after 5, 10, 20 years when compound growth kicks in massively.

slides.title: What You Learned: Mutual Funds & SIP
slides.storyContext: Priya now has an SIP in place. Every month, ₹500 is automatically invested. She doesn't stress about stock picks. She knows that over 10 years, compound growth will turn her ₹60,000 into ₹70,000+. Simple.

points.text: Mutual fund = Many investors pool money; experts manage it; you own units and share gains.
NAV = Daily price of one unit. Buy at low NAV, sell at high NAV, make profit.
SIP = Invest fixed amount (₹500) every month. Automatic, disciplined, removes emotion.
Rupee cost averaging = Buying more units when NAV is low, fewer when NAV is high, lowers your average cost.
Diversification = Own many stocks via mutual fund. If one fails, others protect you.
Compound growth = Early investments grow for years. ₹72,000 invested over 20 years can become ₹200,000+.
Start young, invest small, stay consistent. Time is your superpower.
Choose fund type (Equity/Debt/Balanced) based on your time horizon: 10+ years = Equity; 2-5 years = Debt; 5-10 = Balanced.
Expense ratio matters: 2% fees vs. 0.5% can cost you ₹25,000+ over 10 years. Choose low-cost funds.
SIP beats lump sum in volatile markets; lump sum beats SIP in steady uptrends. For safety, SIP is best.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mutual funds + SIP = The easiest way for ordinary Indians to grow wealth without becoming stock experts or having large lump sums.

image.alt: What You Learned: Mutual Funds & SIP — Mutual Funds & SIP — Investing Made Simple

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade
title: Arjun's Grandma's Gold: Why People Invest in Real Assets
hook: Arjun's grandmother owns gold jewelry. Is it just for beauty, or is it an investment? Let's explore commodities.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Curious about why his grandma hoards gold

characters.name: Dadi (Grandmother)
characters.role: Owns gold; believes in real assets

slides.title: Gold & Commodities
slides.storyContext: Arjun notices his Dadi (grandmother) has gold jewelry in a locker. She says it's her 'emergency fund.' But why gold? Why not money in the bank? Let's find out.

image.alt: Gold & Commodities — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Why Does Dadi Keep Gold?
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks his Dadi: 'Why do you keep gold locked away? Why not keep money in the bank?' Dadi smiles: 'Beta, I've seen times when money's value changes, but gold always has value. In India, we've trusted gold for 2,000 years.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Gold has been valuable forever. People use it as 'real money' that doesn't depend on any government or bank. It's real, tangible, trusted.

image.alt: Why Does Dadi Keep Gold? — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Arjun's Research: Asking Around
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks his friends: 'Does anyone's family have gold?' Almost everyone says yes! He talks to Priya, who says: 'My mom says gold is insurance against currency crashing. If rupees become worthless, we still have gold.' This intrigues Arjun.
slides.inSimpleWords: In India, holding gold is cultural AND financial. It's been passed down for generations as 'real wealth' that survives crises.

slides.title: What are Commodities?
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor explains: 'A commodity is any real, physical thing that has value and is bought and sold. Gold is one. But there are others: oil, wheat, sugar, cotton, copper.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A commodity is a raw material or product that is bought and sold in large quantities. It has real, physical form. Wheat, oil, gold, copper, coffee—all are commodities.

points.label: Why commodities matter
points.text: Economies run on commodities. Farmers need wheat seeds. Factories need copper and oil. Countries need gold reserves. Commodities are the backbone.

points.label: Commodities vs. stocks
points.text: Stocks = ownership of a company. Commodities = raw materials or goods. Stocks can fall to zero (if company fails). Commodities are physical and always have some value.

slides.inSimpleWords: Commodities are real things you can touch: gold, wheat, oil, coffee. They're different from stocks (company ownership) or money (just paper).

image.alt: What are Commodities? — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Mr. Kapoor's Explanation: Why Commodities Are Different
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor asks: 'Why would a country's central bank hold gold instead of dollars?' Arjun thinks... then Mr. Kapoor explains: 'Because gold never becomes worthless. Currencies can be printed unlimited times. Gold is finite.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A government can print unlimited rupees or dollars. But it can't print gold. Gold's scarcity makes it trustworthy across generations.

slides.title: Example: Why Commodities Are Different From Stocks
slides.storyContext: Arjun wonders: If I buy a stock and the company fails, I lose everything. What if I buy gold and... well, I still have gold. Is that safer?

example.problem:
Arjun buys ₹10,000 of TechCorp stock. The company makes bad products, loses customers, and goes bankrupt. His stock is worthless (₹0).

Arjun's Dadi buys 100 grams of gold for ₹5,000/gm (total ₹5 lakh). Gold 'goes out of fashion' temporarily (hypothetically). Gold is still worth ₹4,500/gm. Her ₹5 lakh investment is now ₹4.5 lakh.

Who lost more in percentage terms?
example.solution:
Arjun: Lost ₹10,000 (100% loss).
Dadi: Lost ₹5,000 per gram = ₹5,00,000 total loss. But as a percentage: (5 lakh - 4.5 lakh) / 5 lakh = 10% loss. Dadi's gold is still worth ₹4.5 lakh—she can still sell it, buy food, pay rent. Arjun's stock is worthless. Key: Gold never goes to zero. Stocks can.

slides.inSimpleWords: A stock can become worthless if the company fails. Gold is physical—even if no one wants it temporarily, you can melt it or sell it for something. It always has value.

slides.title: Why People Invest in Gold
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor asks the class: 'Why is gold special among all commodities?' Arjun's hand goes up. His Dadi taught him well.

points.label: Universal value
points.text: Every culture, every country respects gold. You can sell gold anywhere in the world. No country's gold is 'bad'—all 24-carat gold is the same.

points.label: Hedge against inflation
points.text: If inflation is 6% and your bank gives 3% interest, your savings lose value. Gold typically rises with inflation. If inflation hits 8%, gold price often rises, protecting your wealth.

points.label: Hedge against currency risk
points.text: If the rupee weakens (₹ loses value), gold in rupees becomes more expensive. But you still own real gold. Your wealth isn't dependent on currency strength.

points.label: Cultural and emotional reasons
points.text: In India, gold is given as gifts, used in weddings, and worn for status. This cultural demand keeps gold valuable.

points.label: No default risk
points.text: A bank can fail (though rare), and you lose deposits. Gold is yours physically. A government can't print more real gold.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gold is like 'real money' that doesn't depend on any bank or government. Everyone trusts it. If rupees weaken or prices rise, gold rises with it.

image.alt: Why People Invest in Gold — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Arjun's Question: But Gold Doesn't Earn Interest
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Gold sits in a locker. It doesn't earn interest like a bank account. Why not just keep money in the bank?' Mr. Kapoor nods: 'Good point. But banks earn you 3-4% while inflation is 6%. You're losing money. Gold rises with inflation, protecting you.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The real question: Do you want 'safe' money that loses buying power, or 'risky' money that keeps its value? Gold keeps value; banks lose to inflation.

slides.title: Example: Gold as Inflation Hedge
slides.storyContext: In 2000, inflation in India was 4% yearly. A kilogram of gold cost ₹6,000. A bank gave 5% interest. Fast forward to 2024: inflation averaged 6% yearly, and gold costs ₹75,000/kg. Who kept more wealth: someone who held cash in the bank or someone who held gold?

example.problem:
2000: Person A puts ₹6,000 in bank (5% interest). Person B buys 1 kg gold at ₹6,000.

2024 (24 years later):
Person A: ₹6,000 × (1.05)^24 (compounded yearly) ≈ ₹19,530. But inflation has run at 6% on average. What could ₹6,000 buy in 2000 would cost ₹6,000 × (1.06)^24 ≈ ₹24,647 in 2024. Person A's real wealth = ₹19,530 / ₹24,647 worth of 'goods' = he's lost value.

Person B: 1 kg gold at ₹75,000. Adjusted for inflation, same goods now cost 4.1× more (₹24,647 / ₹6,000). Gold went from ₹6,000 to ₹75,000 (12.5x). Person B's real wealth has GROWN.

Who protected their wealth better?
example.solution: Person B (gold). Gold at 12.5x vs. bank at 3.25x (19,530/6,000). Gold outpaced inflation massively. Even accounting for inflation, gold preserved and grew wealth. The bank's 5% interest couldn't beat the 6% inflation.

slides.inSimpleWords: If inflation is 6% and banks give 4%, your cash loses buying power yearly. Gold typically rises with inflation, protecting and growing your wealth.

slides.title: How Supply and Demand Set Commodity Prices
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor draws a supply-demand curve: 'The price of any commodity, including gold, is set by how much people want it vs. how much is available.'

points.label: High demand + Low supply
points.text: Everyone wants gold, but only so much is mined each year. Price rises. Example: During economic crises, people rush to buy gold. Prices jump.

points.label: Low demand + High supply
points.text: If interest rates are very high, people prefer fixed deposits over gold (can't hold gold in hand). Demand falls. If mining increases supply, price falls.

points.label: Global factors
points.text: Major gold mines are in Australia, China, Russia, USA. Political unrest there affects supply. Central banks (RBI, US Fed) buy gold when they need reserves; that demand affects price.

points.label: Real example (Oil)
points.text: In 2020, oil demand crashed during COVID lockdowns. Oil prices fell 30-50%. In 2022, Russia-Ukraine war disrupted supplies. Oil prices jumped 60%+.

slides.inSimpleWords: Commodity prices move up and down based on who wants it and how much is available. War, politics, weather, and economic news all affect supply and demand.

image.alt: How Supply and Demand Set Commodity Prices — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Example: Gold Price Spikes During Crisis
slides.storyContext: March 2020: COVID lockdowns hit. Stock market crashes. People panic. Everyone buys gold for safety. Supply of gold doesn't change, but demand explodes. What happens to price?

example.problem:
Before COVID: Gold supply is stable at 3,000 tons/year globally. Annual demand ≈ 3,500 tons (demand exceeds supply, price rises gradually).

COVID outbreak: Stock market falls 30%. People panic. Gold demand surges to 4,500 tons. Supply stays at 3,000 tons.

What happens to gold price? (Use supply-demand logic.)
example.solution: Demand jumped 1,000 tons (4,500 - 3,500). Supply is fixed. Shortfall = 1,500 tons (4,500 demand - 3,000 supply). Buyers compete to buy limited gold. Price rises. If gold was ₹50,000/gm before, it might spike to ₹55,000-60,000/gm as panic-buyers pay higher prices to secure gold. This actually happened in March 2020—gold prices hit all-time highs.

slides.inSimpleWords: When everyone wants gold at once and supply is fixed, prices shoot up. This is why gold is called a 'crisis hedge'—it rises when stocks crash.

image.alt: Example: Gold Price Spikes During Crisis — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Gold Price: How Is It Decided?
slides.storyContext: Arjun's mom asks the jeweler: 'Why does gold price change every day?' The jeweler says: 'International markets decide it. We follow the global rate.'

points.label: London Bullion Market
points.text: The world's largest gold trading market. Prices are set here twice daily (morning and afternoon fixes). This price is in USD per ounce.

points.label: Conversion to Indian rupees
points.text: International price is in USD. Indian jewelers convert it to rupees using the day's USD-INR exchange rate. So gold price in ₹ depends on both gold demand AND rupee strength.

points.label: Jeweler's margin
points.text: The shop's buying price and selling price are different. They add a margin for making charges, taxes (GST 5%), and profit.

points.label: Making charges
points.text: Converting raw gold into jewelry requires labor and skill. Jewelers charge 6-10% for making and design. So if gold costs ₹60,000/gm, jewelry costs ₹63,600-66,000/gm.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gold price in India = (World gold price in USD) × (USD-INR exchange rate) + (Making charges & taxes). So gold prices tied to both global demand and rupee strength.

image.alt: Gold Price: How Is It Decided? — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Example: How Exchange Rate Affects Gold Price in India
slides.storyContext: Gold is priced globally in USD. But Arjun's Dadi buys in rupees. What happens when the rupee weakens?

example.problem:
Global gold price = $1,800 per ounce (fixed).
Exchange rate changes:
Scenario A: 1 USD = ₹80 (rupee is strong). Gold price in India = 1,800 × 80 = ₹1,44,000/ounce.
Scenario B: 1 USD = ₹85 (rupee weakens). Gold price in India = 1,800 × 85 = ₹1,53,000/ounce.

If Arjun's Dadi wants to buy gold in Scenario B, does she pay more or less in rupees? Why?
example.solution: She pays more in rupees (₹1,53,000 vs. ₹1,44,000). The gold's global price didn't change ($1,800), but the rupee weakened. Each dollar now costs 5 more rupees. So she needs 5 more rupees to buy the same gold. Weak rupee = imported goods (including gold) cost more in rupees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Weak rupee = gold costs more in rupees. Strong rupee = gold costs less in rupees. Your gold price in India depends on global gold price AND rupee strength.

image.alt: Example: How Exchange Rate Affects Gold Price in India — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Real Gold Price Example: Dadi's Gold Investment
slides.storyContext: Dadi bought 10 grams of gold jewelry in 2010 for ₹15,000/gm (total ₹150,000). Today, in 2024, gold is ₹75,000/gm. How much is her investment worth?

example.problem:
Dadi's Gold Investment:
- Bought: 10 grams in 2010 at ₹15,000/gm = ₹150,000 total
- Today's price: ₹75,000/gm
- Today's value of 10 grams = ?
- Gain = ?
- What's the annual return?
example.solution:
Today's value = 10 × ₹75,000 = ₹750,000.
Gain = ₹750,000 - ₹150,000 = ₹600,000 (400% gain!).
Time period = 14 years.
Annual return ≈ (₹750,000 / ₹150,000) ^ (1/14) - 1 ≈ 10% per year.
Comparison: If Dadi had kept ₹150,000 in a bank at 4% interest, she'd have ₹270,000 today. Gold gave her ₹750,000. Difference: ₹480,000 extra!

slides.inSimpleWords: Gold bought in 2010 for ₹150,000 is now worth ₹750,000. That's roughly 10% annual returns—way better than bank interest. This is why Dadi loves gold.

image.alt: Real Gold Price Example: Dadi's Gold Investment — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Other Commodities: Wheat, Oil, Copper, Cotton
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor says: 'Gold is special, but farmers invest in wheat futures, countries invest in oil reserves, and companies invest in copper. Let's see how.'

points.label: Agricultural commodities (Wheat, Sugar)
points.text: Farmers and governments buy/sell these for food security. Prices depend on harvest, weather, global demand. India exports wheat to many countries.

points.label: Energy commodities (Oil, Natural Gas)
points.text: Crucial for electricity, transport, manufacturing. OPEC (oil-producing countries) controls supply. Price swings affect everything—petrol, electricity, inflation.

points.label: Metal commodities (Copper, Aluminum)
points.text: Used in construction, electronics, cars. When economy is strong, demand rises (prices up). When economy is weak, demand falls (prices down).

points.label: Example: India's perspective
points.text: India imports most oil (₹10+ lakh crore/year). If oil prices fall, India saves money → inflation falls, economy grows. If oil prices spike, inflation rises, growth suffers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every country needs commodities: food, energy, metals. Prices rise and fall based on weather, politics, and global demand. Smart investors watch these.

image.alt: Other Commodities: Wheat, Oil, Copper, Cotton — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Arjun's Dad Explains Oil Prices' Impact
slides.storyContext: Arjun's dad says: 'My company's profit depends on oil prices. When oil is expensive, shipping costs rise, margins fall. Oil prices are like the heartbeat of the economy.' Arjun realizes: commodities touch everyone.
slides.inSimpleWords: Commodity prices ripple through the economy. Oil, wheat, copper—they affect your job, your company's profit, and your living costs.

slides.title: Example: Oil Price Crash and India's Benefit
slides.storyContext: In early 2020, during COVID, oil prices crashed from $60/barrel to $20/barrel (70% drop). India imports 70% of its oil needs. How did this benefit India's economy?

example.problem:
India's annual oil imports ≈ 250 million barrels.
Before crash: 250M barrels × $60 = $15 billion.
After crash: 250M barrels × $20 = $5 billion.
Savings = $10 billion annually.

How does this help India's economy?
example.solution: India saved $10 billion on oil imports. This money can be used for: (1) Government invests in infrastructure, schools, hospitals. (2) Inflation falls—petrol/diesel prices drop, everything becomes cheaper. (3) Consumers have more money to spend, boosting economy. (4) Forex reserves increase (less money going abroad). Real impact: When crude oil prices fell in 2020, India's inflation fell from 7% to 2.5%, and the economy handled COVID better than expected.

slides.inSimpleWords: When oil prices crash, India (an importer) benefits: cheaper petrol, lower inflation, stronger economy. When oil prices spike, India suffers: expensive petrol, high inflation, slow growth.

slides.title: How to Invest in Commodities (Without Buying Physical Gold)
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Do I have to buy gold jewelry? Can I invest in gold without wearing it?' Yes! Mr. Kapoor explains modern ways.

points.label: Gold ETFs (Exchange-Traded Funds)
points.text: A fund that holds physical gold. You buy units. Price tracks gold. Easier than buying jewelry, no making charges, very liquid (easy to sell).

points.label: Gold Bonds (Sovereign Gold Bonds)
points.text: Government-issued bonds backed by gold. You get interest + gold appreciation. Issued periodically. Safer than buying from shops.

points.label: Gold Futures & Derivatives
points.text: Advanced: You bet on gold prices without owning gold. High risk, needs expertise. Not for beginners.

points.label: Digital Gold Apps
points.text: Apps like SafeGold let you buy gold in small amounts (even ₹100) digitally. Stored in vaults. Can sell anytime. Very convenient.

slides.inSimpleWords: You don't need to buy physical jewelry to invest in gold. ETFs, government bonds, and apps let you own gold digitally without storage worry.

image.alt: How to Invest in Commodities (Without Buying Physical Gold) — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Example: Gold ETF vs. Physical Gold
slides.storyContext: Priya wants to invest ₹10,000 in gold. She can buy physical jewelry (₹10,000 ÷ ₹75,000/gm = 0.133 gm of jewelry) or a gold ETF. Let's compare.

example.problem:
Physical Gold: Priya buys 0.133 gm of gold jewelry for ₹10,000 (includes making charges & taxes).
- Locked in a locker (security)
- Must go to jeweler to sell (takes time)
- If she sells, loses making charges again (6-10%)

Gold ETF: Priya buys ₹10,000 of gold ETF units.
- Held in demat account (digital, safe)
- Can sell instantly online
- No making charges (1-2% expense ratio only)

After 1 year, gold price rises from ₹75,000/gm to ₹82,000/gm (9.3% gain). She sells both. How much does she net?
example.solution:
Physical Gold: 0.133 × ₹82,000 = ₹10,906 gross. But selling loses 8% making charges = ₹10,906 × 0.92 ≈ ₹10,034 net. Gain ≈ ₹34 (0.3%).

Gold ETF: ₹10,000 grows 9.3% to ₹10,930. Minus 1.5% expense ratio = ₹10,930 × 0.985 ≈ ₹10,766 net. Gain ≈ ₹766 (7.7%).

Gold ETF wins by ₹732. No making charges, instant liquidity, lower costs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gold ETFs beat jewelry if you're investing, not wearing. No making charges, easier to sell, lower costs. Jewelry is good only if you also want to wear it.

image.alt: Example: Gold ETF vs. Physical Gold — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Your Turn: Commodity Price Detective
slides.storyContext: Imagine it's 2030. You're a financial analyst. Oil prices have jumped 40% due to a conflict in the Middle East. Wheat prices fell 20% due to a bumper harvest in India and Russia. Gold price rose 15% as investors panic. What does this mean for: (a) Petrol prices in India? (b) Food prices? (c) Currency (rupee)? (d) Your mutual fund that holds these stocks?

example.problem:
Commodity Crisis in 2030:
1. Oil up 40% → Petrol prices: up or down? By how much? (Assume oil is 50% of petrol cost)
2. Wheat down 20% → Bread, flour prices: up or down? By how much?
3. Gold up 15% → Rupee: strengthen or weaken? Why?
4. Your equity mutual fund holds oil companies (down due to high costs) and exporters (hurt by weak rupee) → Fund value: up or down?
example.solution:
1. Petrol up ~20% (0.4 × 50% of cost). Gas stations suffer. Your gas bills rise ₹5-10 per liter.
2. Wheat down 20% → Bread, flour down ~10-15%. Groceries become cheap. Good for consumers. Bad for farmers.
3. Gold up, rupee likely weakens. Reason: If there's global panic, investors flee to gold (risk-off), they sell rupees → rupee weakens. 1 USD might become ₹92 from ₹83.
4. Mutual fund likely DOWN. Oil companies' profits fall (high input costs). Export companies hit by weak rupee (earn less in rupees). Maybe IT companies (dollar earners) rise, but overall: DOWN ~5-10%.
Key: Commodities ripple through the entire economy. Watchful investors see these signals and adjust.

slides.inSimpleWords: Commodity prices affect everything—your petrol bills, grocery costs, job security (if company exports), and your investments. Smart people watch commodity prices like a weather forecast.

image.alt: Your Turn: Commodity Price Detective — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Challenge: Hedging with Gold and Commodities
slides.storyContext: You have ₹5 lakh in stocks (equity mutual fund). You're worried about an economic crash. You decide to put 20% (₹1 lakh) into gold as a 'hedge.' If stocks crash 30% but gold rises 20%, what's your portfolio value? Is the hedge worth it?

example.problem:
Portfolio Before: ₹4 lakh stocks + ₹1 lakh gold = ₹5 lakh total.

Scenario: Stock market crashes 30%, gold rises 20%.
- Stocks: ₹4 lakh → ₹4 lakh × (1 - 0.30) = ₹2.8 lakh
- Gold: ₹1 lakh → ₹1 lakh × 1.20 = ₹1.2 lakh
- Total = ₹4 lakh

If you had 100% stocks (no hedge):
- ₹5 lakh × 0.70 = ₹3.5 lakh

Which did better, and by how much?
example.solution: With hedge: ₹4 lakh. Without hedge: ₹3.5 lakh. Difference: ₹0.5 lakh (₹50,000 saved). The 20% gold hedge (meant for 'stability') actually saved ₹50,000 in a crash. The hedge worked because gold and stocks move opposite directions—when stocks crash from fear, investors buy gold. This is why Dadi keeps gold: it's not about returns; it's about having something safe when everything else falls.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gold doesn't grow as fast as stocks, but it doesn't crash with stocks. In a portfolio, 10-20% gold is like an insurance policy—it protects your wealth in a crisis.

image.alt: Challenge: Hedging with Gold and Commodities — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

slides.title: Gold in Your Portfolio: Finding the Right Balance
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor explains: 'Gold is important, but it shouldn't be your entire portfolio. Most investors mix stocks, gold, bonds, and cash. The mix depends on your age and goals.'

points.label: Young investors (15-30 years old)
points.text: 10% gold, 70% stocks, 10% bonds, 10% cash. Time to recover from crashes. Mostly stocks for growth.

points.label: Mid-age investors (30-50 years old)
points.text: 15-20% gold, 60% stocks, 15% bonds, 10% cash. More caution. Stable gold provides safety.

points.label: Pre-retirement (50-65 years old)
points.text: 20-30% gold, 40-50% stocks, 20% bonds, 10% cash. Gold hedges retirement risk. Less stock volatility.

points.label: Retired investors (65+ years old)
points.text: 30-40% gold, 20-30% stocks, 30% bonds, 10-20% cash. Gold generates steady income. Minimal volatility.

slides.inSimpleWords: The more time you have, the more stocks you can hold. As you age and have less recovery time, increase gold and bonds for safety.

slides.title: Arjun's Realization: Why His Dadi Is Right
slides.storyContext: Arjun thinks about his Dadi's gold, then about his mutual fund investing. He realizes: 'Dadi's holding 20% gold as insurance. I'm holding 70% stocks for growth. We're both right—at different life stages!' Mr. Kapoor nods: 'Exactly. Wisdom means knowing what mix is right for YOU.'
slides.inSimpleWords: There's no single right investment. Young = more risk (stocks). Old = more safety (gold, bonds). The trick is knowing which you are and staying disciplined.

slides.title: Risks of Commodity Investing
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor cautions: 'Gold and commodities aren't risk-free. They can be volatile, have storage/insurance costs, and don't generate income like stocks or bonds.'

points.label: Price volatility
points.text: Gold can swing 10-20% in a year. Impatient investors panic-sell at lows. Long-term investors ride out swings.

points.label: No income/interest
points.text: Gold doesn't pay dividends or interest. Your only return is price appreciation. Stocks and bonds pay income.

points.label: Storage and insurance costs
points.text: Physical gold in a locker costs ~0.5-1% per year for security and insurance. Digital gold (ETFs) costs 1-2%.

points.label: Geopolitical risk
points.text: Gold prices can spike or crash on global news (war, interest rates, dollar strength). Unpredictable.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gold is stable long-term, but short-term volatility tests patience. Costs (storage, insurance) eat into gains. It's not a get-rich-quick asset.

slides.title: Dadi's Wisdom on Wealth
slides.storyContext: Dadi tells Arjun: 'Beta, I learned long ago that not all wealth should be in paper or numbers on a computer. Real things—gold, land—these hold their worth when everything else shakes.' Arjun now understands.
slides.inSimpleWords: Real assets (gold, land, commodities) are like anchors. When paper money or stocks falter, real assets keep their value. This is the secret wealth preservation.

slides.title: What You Learned: Gold & Commodities
slides.storyContext: Now Arjun understands why his Dadi keeps gold. She's not just following tradition—she's making a smart, long-term investment. Gold and commodities are real assets that protect wealth.

points.text: Commodity = Real physical good (gold, wheat, oil, copper) bought and sold in quantity.
Gold = Ultimate hedge against inflation and currency weakness. Universal value.
Supply & Demand = Commodity prices set by how much is available vs. how much people want.
Gold price in India = (World price in USD) × (USD-INR rate) + making charges + taxes.
Dadi's gold bought at ₹15,000/gm in 2010 is now ₹75,000/gm. That's ~10% annual returns, far better than banks.
Oil, wheat, copper prices affect inflation, petrol costs, food costs, exports, and your mutual fund.
You can invest in gold via ETFs, gold bonds, or digital apps—no need to buy jewelry and pay making charges.
Real assets (gold, commodities) are wealth insurance when currency or stocks falter. 10-20% gold in your portfolio hedges risk.
Gold rises during crisis (stocks fall). This negative correlation makes gold a perfect portfolio hedge.
For long-term wealth, mix: 70% stocks/mutual funds + 20% gold/commodities + 10% bonds/cash. This balanced portfolio handles any economic season.

slides.inSimpleWords: Gold and commodities are real assets that have held value for centuries. They protect you when money loses value. Dadi was wise all along.

image.alt: What You Learned: Gold & Commodities — Gold & Commodities — Real Things People Trade

subject: Mathematics
title: Raj's Railway Ticket Mystery
hook: Raj discovers that numbers hide deep secrets at a railway station.

image.alt: Real Numbers: Order and Divisibility — Real Numbers

slides.title: At the Railway Station
slides.storyContext: Raj is queuing for tickets at Delhi Railway Station. The station master Mr. Sharma is distributing 240 and 180 tickets equally among different counters. Raj wonders: what is the largest number of counters that can receive equal tickets?

image.alt: At the Railway Station — Real Numbers

slides.title: What Are Real Numbers?

points.label: Real Numbers
points.text: All numbers on the number line: natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rationals (fractions), and irrationals (like √2, π).

points.label: Examples
points.text: 5 (natural), 0 (whole), -3 (integer), 1/2 (rational), √7 (irrational)

points.label: Order Property
points.text: Real numbers can be compared: 2 < 5, -1 < 0, 0.5 > 0.4

slides.inSimpleWords: Real numbers are all the numbers you can place on a line, including whole numbers and fractions.

image.alt: What Are Real Numbers? — Real Numbers

slides.title: Euclid's Division Lemma

points.label: Definition
points.text: For any two positive integers a and b, there exist unique integers q and r such that a = bq + r, where 0 ≤ r < b.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing a larger number by a smaller one always leaves a remainder smaller than the divisor.

image.alt: Euclid's Division Lemma — Real Numbers

slides.title: Raj Helps the Station Master
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma tells Raj: 'I have 240 morning tickets and 180 evening tickets to distribute equally across counters. Each counter must get the same number of both types.' Raj realizes this is a divisibility problem! He needs to find the largest number that divides both 240 and 180.

image.alt: Raj Helps the Station Master — Real Numbers

points.label: HCF(240, 180) = 60
points.text: The station can use 60 counters, each getting 4 + 3 = 7 tickets total.

example.problem: Find HCF(455, 130)

image.alt: Finding HCF using Euclid's Algorithm — Real Numbers

example.problem: Find HCF(560, 210) using Euclid's Division Lemma

image.alt: Practice: Euclid's Algorithm Step-by-Step — Real Numbers

slides.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic

points.label: Theorem
points.text: Every integer greater than 1 is either prime or can be uniquely expressed as a product of primes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Any number can be broken into prime building blocks in only one way.

image.alt: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic — Real Numbers

slides.title: Prime Factorization at the Station
slides.storyContext: Priya joins Raj at the station. She asks Mr. Sharma: 'Can we also find HCF by breaking down the numbers into primes?' Mr. Sharma nods and Priya writes: 240 = 2⁴ × 3 × 5 and 180 = 2² × 3² × 5. They pick the smallest power of each common prime to find HCF = 2² × 3 × 5 = 60. Same answer!

image.alt: Prime Factorization at the Station — Real Numbers

example.problem: Prime factorize 84 and 126, then find HCF

image.alt: Prime Factorization Practice — Real Numbers

points.label: Formula
points.text: For any two numbers a and b: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b

example.problem: If HCF(12, 18) = 6, find LCM(12, 18)

image.alt: HCF × LCM Property — Real Numbers

example.problem: Two buses leave Delhi station together at 6 AM. Bus A returns every 90 minutes, Bus B every 150 minutes. When will both be at the station together again?
example.solution: Find LCM(90, 150). 90 = 2 × 3² × 5; 150 = 2 × 3 × 5². LCM = 2 × 3² × 5² = 450 minutes = 7.5 hours. Answer: 1:30 PM.

image.alt: Challenge: Bus Schedule (LCM Application) — Real Numbers

slides.title: Proving √2 is Irrational

points.label: Assume
points.text: √2 = p/q where p, q are coprime integers (HCF = 1)

points.label: Square
points.text: 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q²

points.label: Conclusion
points.text: This means p² is even, so p is even. Let p = 2m. Then 4m² = 2q², so q² = 2m², making q even too.

points.label: Contradiction
points.text: Both p and q are even, contradicting our assumption they were coprime. Therefore √2 is irrational.

slides.inSimpleWords: √2 cannot be written as a fraction of two whole numbers.

image.alt: Proving √2 is Irrational — Real Numbers

slides.title: Priya's Puzzle About √2
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Raj a spiral drawn on paper. 'Can you measure this exactly?' she asks. 'This spiral is made of irrational numbers like √2. No matter how precise your ruler, you can never express √2 as a simple fraction. It's infinite and non-repeating!' Raj is amazed that some real numbers can't be fractions at all.

image.alt: Priya's Puzzle About √2 — Real Numbers

example.problem: Show that √3 is irrational (by contradiction)
example.solution: Assume √3 = p/q (coprime). Then 3 = p²/q², so p² = 3q². This means p² is divisible by 3, so p is divisible by 3. Let p = 3k. Then 9k² = 3q², so q² = 3k², meaning q is also divisible by 3. Contradiction! So √3 is irrational.

image.alt: Irrationality Proof Practice — Real Numbers

points.label: Terminating
points.text: 1/8 = 0.125 (ends after 3 decimal places)

points.label: Non-Terminating Repeating
points.text: 1/3 = 0.333... (repeats forever)

points.label: Rule
points.text: p/q is terminating if q = 2^a × 5^b (only factors 2 and 5)

example.problem: Is 7/80 terminating or repeating?

image.alt: Decimal Expansions: Terminating and Non-Terminating — Real Numbers

example.problem: Write 13/40 as a decimal and determine if it's terminating.
example.solution: 40 = 2³ × 5¹ (only factors 2 and 5), so 13/40 terminates. 13/40 = 0.325

image.alt: Decimal Expansion Practice — Real Numbers

example.problem: For each fraction, say if it's terminating or repeating: (a) 5/16 (b) 7/15 (c) 9/24
example.solution: (a) 16 = 2⁴, so terminating: 0.3125. (b) 15 = 3 × 5 (has factor 3), so repeating: 0.4666... (c) 24 = 2³ × 3 (has factor 3), so repeating. But 9/24 = 3/8, and 8 = 2³, so 0.375 terminates.

image.alt: Challenge: Classify Decimal Types — Real Numbers

slides.title: Mr. Sharma's Final Lesson
slides.storyContext: As Raj leaves the station, Mr. Sharma reflects: 'You see, ticket numbers, bus schedules, prime factorization—they all hide the same mathematical truth. Real numbers order everything in the world. Divisibility is the language of fairness: dividing things equally. And some numbers, like √2, remind us that reality is deeper than simple fractions.' Raj nods, understanding now that mathematics isn't abstract—it's everywhere.

image.alt: Mr. Sharma's Final Lesson — Real Numbers

example.problem: The station master needs to pack 48 mathematics books and 36 science books into identical kits with no books left over. What is the maximum number of kits?
example.solution: Find HCF(48, 36). 48 = 36 × 1 + 12; 36 = 12 × 3 + 0. HCF = 12 kits. Each kit has 48/12 = 4 math books and 36/12 = 3 science books.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Railway Ticket Distribution — Real Numbers

example.problem: Two buses leave a station together at 8 AM. Bus A returns every 120 minutes and Bus B every 180 minutes. When will both buses be at the station together again?
example.solution: Find LCM(120, 180). 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5; 180 = 2² × 3² × 5. LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360 minutes = 6 hours. Answer: 2 PM.

image.alt: Your Turn: Bus Schedule Problem — Real Numbers

slides.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers on the Number Line

points.label: Rational Numbers
points.text: Numbers expressible as p/q (fractions). Example: 1/2, 3/4, -5/3, 0, 7

points.label: Irrational Numbers
points.text: Cannot be expressed as p/q. Example: √2, √3, π, e. Decimal form never terminates or repeats.

points.label: Together
points.text: Rationals and irrationals together form all real numbers, densely filling the entire number line.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real numbers are all rational fractions plus irrational numbers like √2.

image.alt: Rational and Irrational Numbers on the Number Line — Real Numbers

slides.title: Mixed Problems: HCF and LCM Together

example.problem: Two ropes of lengths 60 cm and 90 cm. Cut them into equal pieces with no wastage. Max piece length? How many pieces total?
example.solution: Max length = HCF(60, 90). 60 = 2²×3×5; 90 = 2×3²×5. HCF = 2×3×5 = 30 cm/piece. Total pieces = 60/30 + 90/30 = 2 + 3 = 5 pieces.

image.alt: Mixed Problems: HCF and LCM Together — Real Numbers

example.problem: A school has 504 blue chairs and 392 green chairs. Arrange them in rows with same count of each color, max chairs/row. How many rows?
example.solution: Find HCF(504, 392). 504 = 2³×3²×7; 392 = 2³×7². HCF = 2³×7 = 56 chairs/row. Blue rows: 504/56 = 9. Green rows: 392/56 = 7. Total rows = 16.

image.alt: Challenge: Real-World Divisibility — Real Numbers

example.problem: What do √2, √3, √5, √7 have in common? Are all of them irrational?
example.solution: Yes, √p is irrational for any prime p. Proof: if √p = a/b (coprime), then p = a²/b², so a² = pb², meaning p divides a. Let a = pm. Then p²m² = pb², so pm² = b², meaning p divides b. Contradiction, so √p is irrational.

image.alt: Irrational Sequences and Patterns — Real Numbers

points.text: Real numbers include rationals (fractions) and irrationals (like √2)
Euclid's Division Lemma: a = bq + r (0 ≤ r < b)
HCF (GCD) found using Euclid's algorithm or prime factorization
Fundamental Theorem: every number is a unique product of primes
HCF × LCM = product of two numbers
√2 is irrational (cannot be written as p/q)
p/q terminates only if denominator has only factors 2 and 5

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Garden Design
hook: A student uses polynomials to design the perfect garden layout.

image.alt: Polynomials: Roots and Factors — Polynomials

slides.title: Designing a Rectangular Garden
slides.storyContext: Priya's grandmother has 50 meters of fencing. Priya wants to design a rectangular garden where the area is maximized. She writes: Area = x(25 - x). Arjun says this is a polynomial!

image.alt: Designing a Rectangular Garden — Polynomials

slides.title: Polynomial Definition and Degree

points.label: Definition
points.text: A polynomial in x is p(x) = a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + ... + aₙxⁿ where coefficients are real numbers and n is a non-negative integer.

points.label: Degree
points.text: The highest power of x. Example: p(x) = 2x³ + 5x - 3 has degree 3.

points.label: Types
points.text: Linear (degree 1), Quadratic (degree 2), Cubic (degree 3)

slides.inSimpleWords: A polynomial is an expression with x raised to various powers, combined with numbers.

image.alt: Polynomial Definition and Degree — Polynomials

slides.title: Priya Discovers Polynomial Form
slides.storyContext: Priya writes out her garden equation: if the length is x and the width is (25 - x), then Area = x(25 - x) = 25x - x². She realizes she can expand this—it becomes -x² + 25x + 0. Arjun points out: 'This is a degree-2 polynomial, or quadratic! Every term is a power of x multiplied by a number.'

image.alt: Priya Discovers Polynomial Form — Polynomials

points.label: Definition
points.text: A value r is a zero of p(x) if p(r) = 0.

points.label: Example
points.text: For p(x) = x² - 5x + 6, if x = 2: p(2) = 4 - 10 + 6 = 0. So 2 is a zero.

example.problem: Find a zero of p(x) = x² - 9
example.solution: p(3) = 9 - 9 = 0. So x = 3 is a zero. Also x = -3.

image.alt: Zeros of a Polynomial — Polynomials

slides.title: Garden Zeros: When Area Becomes Zero
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'When is the area zero?' She writes 25x - x² = 0 and factors: x(25 - x) = 0. So x = 0 or x = 25. She realizes: if the length is 0 or 25, there's no garden! The zeros tell us boundary values where the garden collapses.

image.alt: Garden Zeros: When Area Becomes Zero — Polynomials

example.problem: Find the zeros of p(x) = x² + 3x + 2

image.alt: Finding Zeros by Factoring — Polynomials

slides.title: Remainder Theorem

points.label: Theorem
points.text: If polynomial p(x) is divided by (x - a), the remainder is p(a).

points.label: Example
points.text: Divide p(x) = x³ - 2x² + 5 by (x - 1). Remainder = p(1) = 1 - 2 + 5 = 4

slides.inSimpleWords: When dividing a polynomial by (x - a), just plug in a to get the remainder.

image.alt: Remainder Theorem — Polynomials

example.problem: Find the remainder when p(x) = 2x³ + 3x² - x + 5 is divided by (x - 2)
example.solution: By Remainder Theorem, remainder = p(2) = 2(8) + 3(4) - 2 + 5 = 16 + 12 - 2 + 5 = 31

image.alt: Practice: Remainder Theorem — Polynomials

points.label: Theorem
points.text: (x - a) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0.

points.label: Example
points.text: Is (x - 2) a factor of p(x) = x³ - 4x² + 5x - 2? Check: p(2) = 8 - 16 + 10 - 2 = 0. Yes!

example.problem: Show (x + 1) is a factor of p(x) = x³ + 2x² - x - 2

image.alt: Factor Theorem — Polynomials

slides.title: Finding Factors in the Garden
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: 'Your polynomial 25x - x² factors as x(25 - x). Let's check: are x = 0 and x = 25 zeros?' Priya plugs in: 'Yes! So (x - 0) and (x - 25) are factors.' Arjun smiles: 'Because zeros are zeros, the factors are linear terms (x - zero).' This is the Factor Theorem in action.

image.alt: Finding Factors in the Garden — Polynomials

slides.title: Factorization of Quadratic Polynomials

points.label: Method
points.text: For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers whose product is ac and sum is b.

points.label: Example
points.text: x² + 7x + 12: two numbers are 3 and 4 (3×4=12, 3+4=7). So x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)

slides.inSimpleWords: Break a quadratic into two simple factors.

image.alt: Factorization of Quadratic Polynomials — Polynomials

example.problem: Factorize 2x² + 5x + 3
example.solution: Here a=2, b=5, c=3. Product ac = 6. Find two numbers: 2 and 3 (2+3=5, 2×3=6). Split: 2x² + 2x + 3x + 3 = 2x(x+1) + 3(x+1) = (2x+3)(x+1)

image.alt: Factorize Quadratics: Step-by-Step — Polynomials

example.problem: Factorize: (a) x² + 8x + 15 (b) 3x² - 10x + 8
example.solution: (a) Find two numbers: 3 and 5 (sum 8, product 15). So (x+3)(x+5). (b) Product ac=24. Numbers: 4 and 6 (sum 10, product 24). 3x² - 4x - 6x + 8 = x(3x-4) - 2(3x-4) = (x-2)(3x-4)

image.alt: Challenge: Factor Quadratics — Polynomials

points.label: Formula
points.text: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder

points.label: Example
points.text: Divide 2x² + 5x + 2 by x + 2. Quotient = 2x + 1, Remainder = 0. So 2x² + 5x + 2 = (x + 2)(2x + 1)

image.alt: Division Algorithm for Polynomials — Polynomials

example.problem: Divide x³ - 6x² + 11x - 6 by (x - 1)
example.solution: Using synthetic division or long division: x³ - 6x² + 11x - 6 = (x-1)(x² - 5x + 6) = (x-1)(x-2)(x-3). Remainder = 0.

image.alt: Polynomial Long Division — Polynomials

slides.title: Mrs. Gupta's Garden Flourishes
slides.storyContext: Using polynomials, Priya finds that maximum area occurs at x = 12.5 meters (the vertex of the parabola). Mrs. Gupta sets up the garden with length 12.5m and width 12.5m—a square! It gives 156.25 m² of space. 'Polynomials made my garden perfect!' Mrs. Gupta exclaims.

image.alt: Mrs. Gupta's Garden Flourishes — Polynomials

example.problem: Priya's garden area is A(x) = x(25 - x) = 25x - x². What are the zeros? When is area maximized?
example.solution: Zeros: 25x - x² = 0 → x(25 - x) = 0 → x = 0 or x = 25. Maximum at vertex x = 12.5 meters, giving A = 156.25 m².

image.alt: Priya's Garden Area — Polynomials

slides.title: Graphing Polynomials: Shape and Behavior

points.label: Degree 2 (Quadratic)
points.text: U-shaped parabola (opens up if a > 0, down if a < 0)

points.label: Degree 3 (Cubic)
points.text: S-shaped curve, crosses x-axis at up to 3 points

points.label: Zeros as Intercepts
points.text: Zeros are x-intercepts where the graph touches or crosses the x-axis

slides.inSimpleWords: Higher-degree polynomials have more wiggles; zeros are where the curve hits the x-axis.

image.alt: Graphing Polynomials: Shape and Behavior — Polynomials

example.problem: Factorize 2x³ - x² - 5x + 2 completely (if possible)
example.solution: Test rational roots using rational root theorem. After testing: (2x-1)(x² - (x-2)) doesn't work cleanly. Try factoring by grouping or using synthetic division with likely roots. Answer: (2x-1) is a factor if 2(1/8)-(1/4)-5(1/2)+2=0, which requires verification.

image.alt: Complete Factorization — Polynomials

example.problem: Find all zeros of p(x) = x³ - 6x² + 11x - 6
example.solution: Test x = 1: 1 - 6 + 11 - 6 = 0 ✓. So (x-1) is a factor. Divide: (x-1)(x²-5x+6) = (x-1)(x-2)(x-3). Zeros: x = 1, 2, 3

image.alt: Cubic Polynomial Zeros — Polynomials

example.problem: Without dividing, prove (x-3) is a factor of p(x) = x³ - 9x² + 26x - 24
example.solution: Use Factor Theorem: p(3) = 27 - 81 + 78 - 24 = 0. So (x-3) is a factor.

image.alt: Challenge: Prove It's a Factor — Polynomials

example.problem: A shop's profit is P(x) = -x² + 40x - 300, where x = items sold (hundreds). Find break-even points.
example.solution: -x² + 40x - 300 = 0. Divide by -1: x² - 40x + 300 = 0. Discriminant = 1600 - 1200 = 400. x = (40 ± 20)/2 = 30 or 10. Break-even at 1000 or 3000 items.

image.alt: Polynomial Applications in Business — Polynomials

slides.title: Maximum Garden Height
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Gupta asks: 'If I plant flowers in rows, with each row 1 meter apart, how tall should they be to fill the space perfectly?' This leads to optimizing a polynomial h(x) = -0.1x² + 3x, where x is distance. The maximum tells us the perfect height.

image.alt: Maximum Garden Height — Polynomials

example.problem: For ax² + bx + c with roots r₁ and r₂, show that r₁ + r₂ = -b/a and r₁ × r₂ = c/a
example.solution: If r₁, r₂ are roots: a(x-r₁)(x-r₂) = ax² - a(r₁+r₂)x + ar₁r₂. Comparing: -a(r₁+r₂) = b, so r₁+r₂ = -b/a. And ar₁r₂ = c, so r₁r₂ = c/a.

image.alt: Vieta's Formulas for Quadratics — Polynomials

points.text: Polynomial: sum of terms with variables raised to whole number powers
Zero: a value where p(x) = 0, also an x-intercept on the graph
Remainder Theorem: remainder when dividing by (x - a) is p(a)
Factor Theorem: (x - a) is a factor iff p(a) = 0
Quadratic factorization: find two numbers with product ac and sum b
Complete factorization breaks polynomial into linear factors (x - zero)
Graphs of quadratics are parabolas; zeros are where curve crosses x-axis

subject: Mathematics
chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
title: Rohit and Neha's Coffee Shop Plan
hook: Two friends plan to open a cafe and need math to figure out prices and quantities.

slides.title: Pair of Linear Equations: Graphical and Algebraic Solutions

image.alt: Pair of Linear Equations: Graphical and Algebraic Solutions — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Opening a Coffee Shop
slides.storyContext: Rohit and Neha want to open a small cafe in Bangalore. They can spend ₹50,000 on equipment and supplies. Coffee makers cost ₹5,000 each and grinders cost ₹3,000 each. They want 6 items total. How many of each should they buy?

image.alt: Opening a Coffee Shop — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Linear Equation in Two Variables

points.label: Definition
points.text: An equation of the form ax + by + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a, b ≠ 0.

points.label: Example
points.text: Number of items: x + y = 6 (where x = coffee makers, y = grinders)

points.label: Solution
points.text: Any pair (x, y) satisfying the equation. For x + y = 6: (1, 5), (2, 4), (3, 3), etc.

slides.inSimpleWords: An equation with two variables forms a straight line when graphed.

image.alt: Linear Equation in Two Variables — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Setting Up Two Equations
slides.storyContext: Rohit writes two equations from the requirements: 'We need 6 items total: x + y = 6. We have ₹50,000 budget: 5000x + 3000y = 50000. These are two linear equations with two unknowns!' Neha asks: 'So we need to find x and y that work in BOTH equations?' 'Exactly!' Rohit replies.

image.alt: Setting Up Two Equations — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: System of Linear Equations

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two equations: 5000x + 3000y = 50000 (money) and x + y = 6 (count)

points.label: Solution
points.text: The pair (x, y) that satisfies BOTH equations simultaneously.

points.label: Simplified
points.text: Divide first by 1000: 5x + 3y = 50 and x + y = 6

slides.inSimpleWords: Find values of x and y that work in both equations at the same time.

image.alt: System of Linear Equations — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Substitution Method

points.label: Step 1
points.text: From x + y = 6, express y = 6 - x

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Substitute in 5x + 3y = 50: 5x + 3(6 - x) = 50

points.label: Wait
points.text: x = 16 but x + y = 6? This means they can't buy only 6 items for ₹50,000 at these prices.

slides.inSimpleWords: Solve one equation for one variable, then substitute into the other.

image.alt: Substitution Method — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve: 2x + y = 7 and x - y = 2
example.solution: From second: x = y + 2. Substitute into first: 2(y + 2) + y = 7 → 2y + 4 + y = 7 → 3y = 3 → y = 1. Then x = 1 + 2 = 3. Solution: (3, 1)

image.alt: Substitution Method: Step-by-Step — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Given: 5x + 3y = 50 and x + y = 6

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Multiply second by 3: 3x + 3y = 18

example.problem: Solve: 2x + y = 7 and x - y = 2
example.solution: Add: 3x = 9 → x = 3. Substitute: 3 - y = 2 → y = 1. Solution: (3, 1)

image.alt: Elimination Method — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve: 3x + 2y = 13 and 5x - 3y = 1
example.solution: Multiply first by 3: 9x + 6y = 39. Multiply second by 2: 10x - 6y = 2. Add: 19x = 41 → x = 41/19. Substitute back to find y = (13 - 3(41/19))/2.

image.alt: Elimination Method Practice — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

points.label: Unique Solution
points.text: Lines intersect at one point (a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂). Example: 2x + 3y = 12 and x - y = 1

points.label: No Solution
points.text: Lines are parallel (a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂). Example: x + y = 5 and x + y = 10

points.label: Infinite Solutions
points.text: Lines are identical (a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂). Example: 2x + 4y = 6 and x + 2y = 3

image.alt: Types of Solutions — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: A Problem Emerges
slides.storyContext: Mr. Patel the accountant rechecks Rohit and Neha's numbers. 'Your system has no solution,' he says. 'With 6 items costing ₹50,000, the cheapest option (all grinders at 3000 each) costs ₹18,000. The most expensive (all coffee makers) costs ₹30,000. You can't hit ₹50,000 exactly!' The friends realize they need to adjust either the budget or the item count.

image.alt: A Problem Emerges — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Graphical Method

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Plot both lines on a coordinate grid.

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Find the point where lines intersect.

points.label: Example
points.text: For x + y = 6: passes through (0, 6) and (6, 0). For 5x + 3y = 50: passes through (0, 16.67) and (10, 0)

slides.inSimpleWords: Graph both equations and see where the lines cross.

image.alt: Graphical Method — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve graphically: x + y = 5 and 2x - y = 1
example.solution: Plot x + y = 5: (0,5), (5,0). Plot 2x - y = 1: (0,-1), (1,3). Lines intersect at (2, 3). Solution: x = 2, y = 3. Check: 2+3=5 ✓ and 2(2)-3=1 ✓

image.alt: Graphical Solution Example — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve: x + y = 3 and x + y = 5
example.solution: Both lines have the form x + y = constant. They are parallel (same slope). They never intersect, so NO SOLUTION. The system is inconsistent.

image.alt: Challenge: When Lines Are Parallel — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Rohit and Neha Adjust Their Plan
slides.storyContext: Rohit proposes a new budget: ₹32,000 instead of ₹50,000. With x + y = 5 items and 5000x + 3000y = 32000 (simplified: 5x + 3y = 32). Let's solve. From first: y = 5 - x. Substitute: 5x + 3(5-x) = 32 → 5x + 15 - 3x = 32 → 2x = 17 → x = 8.5. Still not a whole number. After more discussion, they settle on: 3 espresso machines and 2 milk frothers for ₹21,000.

image.alt: Rohit and Neha Adjust Their Plan — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Revised: Rohit and Neha want to buy espresso machines (₹8,000 each) and milk frothers (₹2,000 each) totaling ₹32,000 and 5 items. How many of each?
example.solution: Equations: 8x + 2y = 32 (divide by 2: 4x + y = 16) and x + y = 5. From second: y = 5 - x. Substitute: 4x + (5 - x) = 16 → 3x = 11 → x = 11/3 ≈ 3.67. Not whole. Adjust to 8x + 2y = 30 and x + y = 5: y = 5 - x → 8x + 2(5 - x) = 30 → 6x = 20 → x = 10/3. Real solution: 3 espresso + 2 frothers = ₹28,000.

image.alt: Realistic Coffee Shop Problem — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: At a vegetable market, Priya buys 2 kg of tomatoes and 3 kg of onions for ₹170. Neha buys 1 kg of tomatoes and 2 kg of onions for ₹100. Find the price per kg of each.
example.solution: Let x = price of tomato/kg, y = price of onion/kg. Equations: 2x + 3y = 170 and x + 2y = 100. From second: x = 100 - 2y. Substitute: 2(100 - 2y) + 3y = 170 → 200 - 4y + 3y = 170 → y = 30. Then x = 100 - 60 = 40. Tomatoes ₹40/kg, onions ₹30/kg.

image.alt: Your Turn: Market Scenario — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: When to Use Each Method

points.label: Substitution
points.text: Best when one equation is already solved for a variable, or one coefficient is 1.

points.label: Elimination
points.text: Best when coefficients are easy to make equal by multiplying.

points.label: Graphical
points.text: Best to visualize solutions; clearly shows if lines intersect, are parallel, or coincide.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different methods work better for different equations; pick based on what's easiest.

image.alt: When to Use Each Method — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve: 4x + 6y = 8 and 2x + 3y = 4
example.solution: Note: 4x + 6y = 8 is 2(2x + 3y) = 2(4), so it's the same as 2x + 3y = 4. The two equations represent the same line! Infinite solutions of form (x, (4-2x)/3) for any x.

image.alt: Challenge: Infinite Solutions — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.solution: Multiply first by 6: 3x + 2y = 12. Multiply second by 4: x + 2y = 4. Subtract: 2x = 8 → x = 4. Then 2y = 4 - 4 = 0 → y = 0. Solution: (4, 0)

image.alt: Fraction Coefficients in Systems — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: What does the system tell us? 3x + 4y = 12 and 6x + 8y = 24
example.solution: Second equation = 2 × First equation. They represent the same line! Infinitely many solutions: (x, (12-3x)/4) for any x. The system is dependent.

image.alt: Challenge: Dependent Equations — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Asha is twice as old as Priya. In 3 years, their ages will sum to 45. Find current ages.
example.solution: Let A = Asha's age, P = Priya's age. A = 2P and (A+3) + (P+3) = 45. Substitute: (2P+3) + (P+3) = 45 → 3P + 6 = 45 → 3P = 39 → P = 13. Then A = 26. Asha is 26, Priya is 13.

image.alt: Real-Life System: Age Problem — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve using comparison: 3x - y = 5 and 2x + y = 10
example.solution: From first: y = 3x - 5. From second: y = 10 - 2x. Set equal: 3x - 5 = 10 - 2x → 5x = 15 → x = 3. Then y = 10 - 6 = 4. Solution: (3, 4)

image.alt: Comparison Method (Alternative) — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Cafe Opening Day
slides.storyContext: With 3 espresso machines and 2 frothers in place, Rohit and Neha open the cafe. They charge ₹50 per espresso and ₹30 per coffee. After day 1, they earned ₹4,500 from 120 drinks total. How many of each did they sell? This is a real system they must solve!

image.alt: Cafe Opening Day — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve: 50e + 30c = 4500 (revenue) and e + c = 120 (total drinks)
example.solution: From second: c = 120 - e. Substitute: 50e + 30(120 - e) = 4500 → 50e + 3600 - 30e = 4500 → 20e = 900 → e = 45. Then c = 75. They sold 45 espressos and 75 coffees.

image.alt: Challenge: Cafe Revenue System — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

points.text: Linear equation in 2 variables: ax + by + c = 0 (straight line)
System: two equations where both must be satisfied simultaneously
Substitution method: solve one for a variable, substitute in other
Elimination method: multiply to make coefficients equal, then subtract
Three types: unique solution (lines intersect), no solution (parallel), infinite (same line)
Graphical method: plot both lines and find intersection point
Real-world problems often require checking if solutions are whole numbers and make practical sense

image.alt: Quadratic Equations: Roots and Solutions — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Building a Home Swimming Pool
slides.storyContext: Aman's family wants to build a rectangular swimming pool with a 4-meter concrete border around it. The outer dimensions are 20m × 16m. Aman needs to find the inner pool dimensions such that the border area equals the pool area. He discovers this leads to a quadratic equation!

image.alt: Building a Home Swimming Pool — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Quadratic Equation Definition

points.label: Standard Form
points.text: ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0 (if a = 0, it's linear, not quadratic)

points.label: Degree
points.text: Always degree 2 (highest power of x is 2)

slides.inSimpleWords: A quadratic equation has x² as the highest power term.

image.alt: Quadratic Equation Definition — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Meera Explains the Pool Problem
slides.storyContext: Meera sits with Aman and breaks down the problem: 'If the inner pool is x by y, then border area = 20×16 - xy. For balance, border area = xy. So 320 - xy = xy, which gives xy = 160. But we also need another equation! The pool's length and width shrink by 4m on each side, so x = 20-8 and y = 16-8... wait, that's fixed! Let me reframe: if both shrink by d meters, then (20-2d)(16-2d) is the pool area.'

image.alt: Meera Explains the Pool Problem — Quadratic Equations

points.label: Method
points.text: Express ax² + bx + c as (px + q)(rx + s) = 0

example.problem: Solve 2x² - 8x + 6 = 0
